title: SYSK's 12 Days of Christmas… Toys: How Monopoly Works
summary: A 12 Days of Christmas rerun of the Stuff You Should Know episode on how Monopoly works. The hosts trace the game's origins from Lizzie Magie's Landlord's Game and Henry George's Georgism through the Quaker-influenced house rules, Ruth Hoskins, Charles Darrow and Parker Brothers' purchase of the game. They cover the board, tokens, cards, and rules (buying, auctions, houses and hotels, mortgages, jail), strategy and probability (orange properties, utilities, railroads, the three-house rule), and Ralph Anspach's Anti-Monopoly lawsuit against Parker Brothers. Listener mail includes a request for help for a family facing a cancer diagnosis during pregnancy.
topics: Monopoly Mr. Monopoly Rich Uncle Pennybags

segments.title: Cold open teaser
segments.summary: A brief teaser introduces the episode and notes that Mr. Monopoly does not wear a monocle; that is Mr. Peanut.

segments.title: Opening banter and Mr. Monopoly's name
segments.summary: The hosts open the show and banter about whether Mr. Monopoly wears a monocle, and about his full name, Rich Uncle Pennybags, and the Monopoly Companion's name Milbourne Pennybags.

segments.title: Monopoly's origins and the Monopoly Companion
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how supplemental Monopoly history exists and how the game became a cultural institution rather than a simple game explainer.

segments.title: Georgism and Lizzie Magie's Landlord's Game
segments.summary: The hosts explain Henry George's Georgism, a land-tax philosophy, and how Lizzie Magie created The Landlord's Game to demonstrate the evils of land grabbing. She made two sets of rules, one where the winner gets rich and one where the community benefits.

segments.title: Quaker influences and early rules
segments.summary: Quaker friends of Lizzie Magie contributed rules such as fixed property prices instead of auctions and household-object tokens. Magie patented the game, and it spread as a folk game.

segments.title: Ruth Hoskins and the Rayfords
segments.summary: Ruth Hoskins in the Philadelphia and Atlantic City area learned the game from Quaker friends Jesse and Eugene Rayford, who changed rules, then taught it to Todd, who brought it to Charles Darrow.

segments.title: Charles Darrow and Parker Brothers' purchase
segments.summary: Charles Darrow, a Depression-era radiator salesman, sold the copied game at Wanamaker's in Philadelphia. Parker Brothers bought the idea, then paid Lizzie Magie for the patent. Darrow's other game ideas went nowhere.

segments.title: Atlantic City properties and Monopoly's corporate appeal
segments.summary: The board mirrors Atlantic City's real geography and neighborhoods, and the hosts note the Marvin Gardens spelling. They mention the New York Times article Monopoly Goes Corporate by Mary Pilon.
topics: Atlantic City real estate on Monopoly board

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor message break.

segments.title: Monopoly versions and licensed editions
segments.summary: Hundreds of Monopoly versions exist, including Star Wars, Simpsons, UK, and a corporate version, and an upcoming custom-board option. Rich Uncle Pennybags is discussed.

segments.title: Fictional rich characters tangent
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a Forbes list of the wealthiest fictional characters, including Scrooge McDuck, Smaug, and Carlisle Cullen.

segments.title: Monopoly tokens and the 2008 set
segments.summary: The hosts describe the tokens in the 2008 set and their retirements and changes, including the iron replaced by the cat in 2013, the cannon and battleship from the failed game Conflict, and the retired horse and rider and lantern.

segments.title: Components and the play money
segments.summary: The hosts list the box contents: the board, dice, tokens, houses, hotels, cards, title deeds, and play money, including the five hundred dollar bill, and their memories of hoarding cash.

segments.title: Board squares and property counts
segments.summary: The hosts count the board's squares: forty squares, twenty-eight purchasable properties, and special squares like tax, Go, and Jail.

segments.title: Jail, POW Monopoly sets, and war movies
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Jake the Jailbird and the rumor that World War Two POWs were given Monopoly sets for escape maps, comparing German and Japanese camps.

segments.title: Chance and Community Chest cards
segments.summary: The hosts describe Chance and Community Chest cards, including street repairs, and mention Lizzie Magie's Game of Life comment.

segments.title: Other board games from childhood
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Game of Life, Yahtzee, Bull, Candy Land, Chutes and Ladders, Operation, Battleship, and Risk.

segments.title: Starting a game and the goal
segments.summary: The hosts describe starting a game: selecting a banker, distributing money, and the goal of bankrupting everyone. They describe Go bonus house rules and the Free Parking jackpot house rule.

segments.title: Auctions and completing color groups
segments.summary: If a player declines to buy a property, it goes to auction, and the banker and the player who declined can bid. The hosts explain monopolies, double rent, and building houses and hotels.

segments.title: Mortgages and personal loans
segments.summary: The hosts explain mortgaging rules: sell hotels back to the bank at half price, then mortgage, and repay the mortgage plus ten percent. They discuss personal loans as a house rule.

segments.title: Candy Land tangent and house rules on trading
segments.summary: The hosts briefly discuss Candy Land and Ticket to Ride, then cover how trades and auctions work on a player's turn.

segments.title: Monopoly World Championship
segments.summary: The hosts mention the Monopoly World Championship held roughly every four years, most recently in 2009, and a North American champion who used the iron token.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor message break.

segments.title: Basic strategy: buy everything and cash hoarding
segments.summary: A strategy guide advises buying every property, keeping little cash, and getting a monopoly even if it is a bad one. The hosts note the three-house rule of thumb.

segments.title: Utilities, Boardwalk and Park Place
segments.summary: The hosts explain why utilities and Boardwalk and Park Place are risky: utilities have variable rent, two properties are landed on less, and they sit before Go.

segments.title: Probabilities and the orange properties
segments.summary: The hosts cite a Scientific American article and a website on probabilities. Orange properties are landed on most often because they follow Jail, and two dice rarely roll a one.

segments.title: Jail rules and strategy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss ways to go to jail and get out, the Get Out of Jail Free card, rolling for doubles, and the strategy of when to pay the fifty dollars.
topics: Get Out of Jail Free card

segments.title: Railroads and personalities in play
segments.summary: Railroads are cheap and pay off when all four are owned. The strategist says the game is about personalities as much as strategy.

segments.title: Ralph Anspach and Anti-Monopoly lawsuit
segments.summary: Economist Ralph Anspach created Anti-Monopoly in the 1970s, sold about two hundred thousand copies, and was sued by Parker Brothers. He fought the case, uncovered the Darrow origin lie, and won at the Supreme Court. He wrote a book about the story. Anti-Monopoly 2 was released in 1984.

segments.title: Longest Monopoly game and closing banter
segments.summary: The hosts mention the longest Monopoly game of seventy days and compare it to a long risk game.

segments.title: How-Stuff-Works article reference and listener mail intro
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to the HowStuffWorks Monopoly rules article and introduce listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: help for a family in need
segments.summary: A listener named Bob from Swarthmore, Pennsylvania writes that his wife has stage four breast cancer while they expect their first child. He asks listeners to follow their Tumblr, support his 150-mile bike ride fundraiser, and send a shout-out to his wife, who works in public policy. The hosts wish them well.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give social media and email contact information and sign off.
